title: Why time seems to accelerate
dek: Childhood summers were long because they were dense with firsts. Routine is a compression algorithm.
speakingPrompts: Describe a week that felt long and a year that vanished. What was different about the density of events?
If novelty slows remembered time, what is one first you could schedule this month without turning life into a stunt?
Explain to a teenager why their holidays feel longer than yours without sounding wistful.

blocks.text: Ask an adult about last autumn and you may get a shrug. Ask them about the autumn they were nine and you may get a landscape. The clocks did not change their manners. The mind’s way of storing intervals did. Several lines of research converge on a blunt idea: time in memory is partly a count of new things.

When you are bored in a queue, time crawls as you watch it. That is prospective time: attention is on duration itself, so seconds are sampled densely. When you look back on a packed year of the same commute, time has thinned. That is retrospective time: the mind infers duration from how much happened, how many distinct episodes can be retrieved. Routine leaves fewer markers. The film is shorter because the editor had less to cut.

Childhood is rich in firsts — first classroom, first betrayal, first map of a town. Adulthood, for many, is a masterpiece of repetition. The proportional theory (a year is a smaller fraction of life at forty than at four) is a popular story and a weaker explanation on its own. You can make a year feel longer at forty by filling it with unmarked days that become marked: a new route, a new skill, a trip that does not resemble last year’s trip.

blocks.title: A scientific caution
blocks.text: Lab studies of duration are not the same as a life story. They do show that attention, emotion, and memory encoding alter estimates. Treat the “busy years fly” remark as a clue about encoding, not as physics.
What to do with a shrinking calendar

You cannot opt out of thermodynamics. You can opt into encoding. Keep the days that matter slightly harder to summarise. Not by manufacturing constant spectacle — that becomes its own blur — but by allowing a few edges: a conversation with someone new, a walk without headphones, a problem you have not already solved. The point is not to live as a tourist. It is to give later-you some landmarks, so the map of the year has more than one road.
